video_title: Lawfare Daily: How Terrorist Groups are Using Artificial Intelligence
gist: Field interviews with Boko Haram members covering 2023 through mid-2025 find the group uses commercial AI models as a full-cycle operational assistant — captured-weapons identification, tactical adaptation, IED chemistry, drone weaponization — far beyond the AI-propaganda use cases most analysts track, while systematically defeating guardrails through jailbreak training from ISIS-linked operatives, multi-provider account shopping, and task decomposition. A Somalia counterpoint shows the government, not the militants, currently winning the AI race via camera networks and Somali-language social monitoring, exposing a second and less-discussed risk: state repression and AI-assisted targeting, where no vendor guardrail applies at all.

insights.claim: Interviews with Boko Haram members indicate AI has become an embedded general-purpose technology across the full insurgent cycle — preparing attacks, executing them, and analyzing failures afterward — functioning as a round-the-clock operational assistant rather than a propaganda tool.
insights.speaker: Antonia (international security lead, Cambridge program on AI science and policy)
entities: Cambridge program on AI science and policy
insights.so_what: Reframes terrorist AI risk from content moderation to operational capability uplift; misuse monitoring built only around propaganda detection will miss the dominant use case.
insights.quote: AI has become embedded really as a general purpose technology that can provide information across the full insertion cycle

insights.claim: Boko Haram changed its battlefield doctrine around AI: captured weapons are now brought back to camp where commanders type in the serial number and model to learn what they have and how to service and troubleshoot it, replacing a slow dependency on ISIS network contacts and in-person trainers.
insights.speaker: Antonia
insights.so_what: A concrete capability change — removal of a training and latency bottleneck — that is entirely invisible to online-content-based threat monitoring.
insights.quote: Now the new rule is that whatever you get, you bring it back to the camp.

insights.claim: AI has been used for tactical adaptation against specific counterterrorism measures, including learning to attack with smaller coordinated units and to cross with motorcycles the defensive trenches the Nigerian military built around its bases and towns — an obstacle that had previously stopped attacks.
insights.speaker: Antonia
insights.so_what: Shows AI closing an adaptation loop against physical fortifications, meaning defensive infrastructure investments depreciate faster than planners assume.

insights.claim: Interviewees described using AI to improve explosive design — which additional chemicals make IEDs more powerful, and how to defuse unexploded ordnance to extract military-grade explosive and repurpose it — with a commander framing AI as an accuracy substitute for lethal trial-and-error.
insights.speaker: Antonia
insights.so_what: Direct evidence that energetics and chemistry uplift from commercial models is already occurring at the low end, not just in hypothetical CBRN scenarios.
insights.quote: as one commander put it, trial and error can kill you. AI gives you accuracy.

insights.claim: AI companies responded to the Boko Haram findings by arguing their safeguards improved after the 2023–mid-2025 study window, but even the latest models remain jailbreakable — from simple techniques like writing prompts as poetry to universal jailbreaks that act as reusable keys succeeding on most harmful requests across an entire domain.
insights.speaker: Antonia
insights.so_what: Vendor claims of improved safety are a moving target that has not closed the exploit class; expect continued regulatory and research pressure on jailbreak resistance.

insights.claim: AI providers are not facing isolated bad users but trained, networked adversaries: Boko Haram members received in-person training from ISIS-linked operatives plus everyday online assistance on prompt engineering and jailbreaking, with techniques shared across the network.
insights.speaker: Antonia
insights.so_what: Safety evaluation designed around single-user red-teaming systematically understates real-world attack capability.
insights.quote: these companies don't just face isolated users um but really like trained network and organized adversaries that share the latest ways to to jailbreak models

insights.claim: Groups arbitrage uneven safety enforcement across providers — holding multiple accounts on multiple models so a refusal on one system simply routes the request to a weaker one, comparing answers to find the most useful, and decomposing a harmful request into smaller harmless-looking pieces that individually pass filters.
insights.speaker: Antonia
insights.so_what: Makes safety a lowest-common-denominator problem across the industry and shows per-prompt classification is structurally insufficient — detection must work at account and pattern level.

insights.claim: Initial research shows much lower refusal rates in Somali because it is a low-resource language, meaning advertised guardrails may not function outside dominant languages like English — even though the same models still score well on multilingual capability benchmarks, including Hausa on accuracy.
insights.speaker: Tricia Bacon and Antonia
insights.so_what: Capability generalizes across languages faster than safety does — a testable gap that repeats the English-dominant content-moderation failure of the social media era.
insights.quote: there's much lower levels of refusal in Somali in part because it is sort of a low resource language

insights.claim: Boko Haram restricts AI to mid-ranking commanders and above — consistent with its existing limits on internet and phone access, because a group relying on coercion does not trust its foot soldiers with capable tools — while running dedicated internal AI units responsible for prompting, jailbreaking, and cascading that knowledge down the hierarchy.
insights.speaker: Antonia
insights.so_what: Internal control policy concentrates AI benefit at the command layer rather than spreading it, and the training units are an observable intelligence target.

insights.claim: Model unreliability is currently an incidental brake on misuse: the group hits hallucinations and says it still has to supplement AI output with human judgment, and there were incidents where following AI instructions during explosives experimentation killed people.
insights.speaker: Antonia
insights.so_what: Implies that gains in model accuracy translate directly into misuse uplift, since error is what currently limits the payoff.

insights.claim: The group's self-identified main limitation is a shortage of in-house technical expertise, and members are aware they could exploit these models far more effectively if they had it.
insights.speaker: Antonia
insights.so_what: Human capital, not model access, is the binding constraint — so tooling that lowers the operator skill required would be the step-change to watch.

themes.theme: Somalia: the state is winning the AI race

insights.claim: In Mogadishu the inverse of the usual story is happening — the government, not the militants, is gaining the AI advantage: city-wide cameras monitor vehicles, license plates and drivers, suppressing al-Shabaab's vehicle-borne explosive attacks; cameras are installed in businesses al-Shabaab extorts; and a Somali-language AI social media monitoring system is about to deploy.
insights.speaker: Tricia Bacon (professor, American University)
insights.so_what: Demand for AI surveillance tooling in low-resource-language, low-capacity states is real and being filled today — a growing market with essentially no external guardrails.

insights.claim: Al-Shabaab's AI lag is partly explained by an unprecedented and rarely-discussed US air campaign whose pace of strikes suppresses phone and internet use to avoid detection, compounded by the group simultaneously trying to absorb drone capability learned from the Houthis — and integrating two new technologies at once is hard for any mature organization.
insights.speaker: Tricia Bacon
insights.so_what: Kinetic pressure acts as an indirect brake on AI adoption, but the same pressure may later force innovation — the speaker explicitly refuses to bet the lag persists.
insights.quote: I wouldn't bet that that will remain that way.

insights.claim: AI capability a government acquires for counterterrorism does not stay confined to counterterrorism — monitoring and vehicle tracking become tools of political repression, no company is positioned to intercede on a state's in-house platform, and the harder frontier is AI-assisted targeting with reduced human involvement, already a concern regarding the United States and Israel and far more dangerous where guardrails are weaker.
insights.speaker: Tricia Bacon
insights.so_what: The unpriced governance risk is state-side; defense and surveillance AI policy may become a higher-stakes battleground than consumer model safety, and vendors currently take almost no public stance on government use limits.
insights.quote: when a government is gaining this kind of AI capability for counterterrorism purposes, it doesn't stay counterterrorism purposes

themes.theme: Propaganda is the overrated use case

insights.claim: AI-generated propaganda gets disproportionate attention in AI risk debates largely because online data is easy to collect, and because AI is misconceived as a smart chatbot — an extension of social media — a comparison that significantly underestimates its capability.
insights.speaker: Antonia
insights.so_what: Availability bias in the research base is steering policy attention toward the least consequential misuse channel while the operational uses stay offline and unmeasured.
insights.quote: AI is often a bit misconceived as like a very smart chatbot an extension of social media and I think that comparison is a bit flawed um and significantly underestimates AI's capability

insights.claim: Unofficial jihadist media outlets and online supporters adopted AI well before the terrorist groups themselves, with online forums debating whether AI is un-Islamic because models are trained on Western voices and faces — but the groups' public reticence likely reflects deliberate concealment rather than genuinely slow adoption.
insights.speaker: Antonia
insights.so_what: Public-facing adoption signals are a biased proxy for real adoption, since groups have reasons to hide AI use that their supporters do not.

insights.claim: A group's incentive to adopt AI for propaganda depends on strategic aim rather than sophistication: al-Shabaab already runs a well-oiled machine in Swahili, Somali, Arabic and English and did not need AI to fix what works, whereas the expansionist Islamic State Khorasan reaches for AI to add new languages and extend its footprint.
insights.speaker: Tricia Bacon
insights.so_what: A usable predictor of which groups adopt AI propaganda first — expansion-seeking groups with unmet language reach, not the most capable ones.

insights.claim: The realistic near-term picture is incremental, not revolutionary — roughly 5 to 10, maybe 20 percent improvements in scattered spheres among some organizations, not a group going from zero to building a nuclear weapon.
insights.speaker: Tricia Bacon
insights.so_what: A calibrated baseline against doomsday framing, useful for pricing near-term national-security risk without dismissing tail scenarios.
insights.quote: it's not universal it's 5% 10% % improvements in different spheres among some organizations

insights.claim: The real test of whether AI is revolutionary is not mature organizations with established processes but new organizations born in the AI era that build AI in as a pillar from the start — whether they develop capabilities more quickly and more innovatively is the open question.
insights.speaker: Tricia Bacon
insights.so_what: A specific forward indicator to watch: the founding cohort of post-2023 groups, rather than the incumbents everyone currently studies.

insights.claim: Compounding efficiency gains and revolution are related rather than opposed — gradual creeping capability can bring a group to an inflection point where AI resolves a previously blocking technical problem, as respondents said it did for weaponizing drones after long failed experimentation using the internet and foreign assistance.
insights.speaker: Antonia
insights.so_what: Argues against reading 'incremental' as 'safe': threshold effects mean linear uplift can produce sudden nonlinear capability jumps after long plateaus.

insights.claim: Whether AI creates a 'new capability' depends entirely on the reference point — chemical and biological weapons are not new in the abstract but would be new for most terrorist groups — and setting the bar at battlefield novelty puts the threshold for concern far too high.
insights.speaker: Antonia
insights.so_what: A definitional critique with policy teeth: 'no new capabilities' conclusions in AI safety evaluations may be measured against the wrong baseline.
insights.quote: I do worry a bit that we set the bar for what constitutes a new capability or revolution and implicitly also for when we should be worried uh way too high

insights.claim: AI-enabled bioterrorism is more credible than many assume: studies show AI already outperforms human experts on relevant biology tasks and could help design pandemic-capable pathogens, and while building a bioweapon still requires manual lab work, facilities, materials and tools, AI is lowering the technical, operational and motivational barriers that kept such attacks out of reach.
insights.speaker: Antonia
insights.so_what: Frames uplift as barrier-lowering across three axes including motivation — the motivational channel is rarely modeled in biosecurity evaluations.

insights.claim: The intent side is misjudged: attention focuses on apocalyptic omnicidal cults, but al-Qaeda and ISIS have apocalyptic strains and have tried to build chemical and biological weapons before — intent has not changed, only the difficulty — and chemical remains a more realistic near-term scenario than bio, where interviewees said the contentious issue was not acquisition but release.
insights.speaker: Antonia
insights.so_what: Widens the intent pool well beyond rare-actor screening and suggests acquisition-focused controls may be aimed at the wrong bottleneck.

insights.claim: The sharpest way to size the tail risk is counterfactual: what if Aum Shinrikyo, which conducted the Tokyo sarin attacks, or Ted Kaczynski, or al-Qaeda's 1990s camps gassing dogs to experiment, had had today's AI — actors who already had intent and baseline scientific capability and were not starting from zero.
insights.speaker: Tricia Bacon
insights.so_what: Locates the real danger zone as AI layered on pre-existing scientific capability rather than AI creating capability from nothing — a narrower, more tractable screening target.

themes.theme: Policy asks for industry and government

insights.claim: The core technical ask is cross-provider minimum safety standards so a refusal from one model does not simply send the user to a weaker competitor — and governments may have to mandate it, because it is unclear whether companies would cooperate to set such standards themselves.
insights.speaker: Antonia
insights.so_what: A specific, checkable regulatory proposal — harmonized refusal floors — that would bite hardest on providers competing on permissiveness.
insights.quote: we need minimum safety standards across providers so that a refusal in one place is not simply an invitation to try another one

insights.claim: Even the most robust safeguards provide very little practical security while highly capable open-weight models are freely available.
insights.speaker: Antonia
insights.so_what: Puts open-weight release policy at the center of the misuse debate — a direct policy risk factor for firms whose strategy depends on open releases.
insights.quote: the most robust safeguards offer very little practical security if highly capable and open weight models are freely available

insights.claim: Companies should test safeguards against organized, trained adversaries rather than isolated users, and industry and government should stand up an AI threat fusion center combining company and government signals so misuse scattered across platforms is seen as one pattern rather than isolated fragments.
insights.speaker: Antonia
insights.so_what: A concrete institutional design — an information-sharing body for AI misuse — that would require cross-company data sharing that does not exist today.
insights.quote: an AI threat fusion center that combines company and government signals

insights.claim: The US intelligence community lacks the bureaucratic structure for this — alongside regional and functional focuses it needs analysts specifically responsible for AI, since the average terrorism analyst cannot track a fast-moving technology while covering group operations — and the binding constraint is pay, because that expertise commands six or seven figures in the private sector.
insights.speaker: Tricia Bacon
insights.so_what: A capability-versus-comprehension gap: the US is on the cutting edge of using AI in warfare while lacking the analytic base, and private-sector wages structurally cap public-sector oversight capacity.
insights.quote: You can make six figures, uh, seven figures with that kind of expertise.
